title: Letters, reports, speeches
examples: When writing a formal letter, what is the correct placement for the date?
How does writing for a child audience change your tone compared to an adult audience?
Can you show me the difference in formatting between a report and a speech?

explain.say: Today we are looking at three different writing styles. You will learn about letters, reports, and speeches.
First we look at letters. A letter needs a clear format to look professional. You must include your address and the recipient's address.
Next we study reports. A report always needs an introduction, clear headings, and a conclusion. You must present evidence to support your points.
Finally, consider speeches. A speech needs an engaging opening, clear main points, and a strong closing statement. You write it to be spoken aloud.

items: Conclusion: Final thought or call to action

explain.say: Now think about your audience. If you write a letter to a scientist, you use formal language. If you write a speech to your friends, you can use more casual words.
A common mistake is forgetting the purpose of the writing. If you write a report, do not include personal feelings. Keep it factual and objective always.

faq.q: Do I always need to use formal language when writing?
faq.a: No, the required language depends on your audience and purpose. A letter to a family member can be informal.
asks: Should I be formal all the time?
When is it okay to sound casual?

faq.q: How much detail should I include in a report?
faq.a: You should include enough detail to support your main findings. Always check if you have enough evidence for your claims.
asks: Is too much detail bad for a report?
How deep should my research go?

faq.q: Does a speech need to sound different when I read it?
faq.a: Yes, a speech is written to be spoken, so it needs rhythm and natural pauses. You should write it like you will actually say it.
asks: Should I write notes for my speech?
How do I make it sound good when I speak?

faq.q: What is the difference between a letter and a report?
faq.a: A letter is usually personal or directed to one person. A report investigates a topic and presents findings to a group.

faq.q: If I write a letter to my principal, should I use contractions?
faq.a: No, for formal writing like a letter to a principal, you should avoid contractions like 'don't' or 'can't'.
asks: Are contractions okay in formal writing?
What is the rule for formal letters?

facts: Letters require specific formatting including addresses and dates.
Reports must maintain an objective tone, relying on evidence.
Speeches are written with the spoken word and audience in mind.
The audience dictates the level of formality in your writing.

quiz.say: Which format is best for presenting factual findings with clear sections?
quiz.why: Reports are specifically designed to organize and present factual findings using headings and evidence.

wrong.0: Letters are primarily for personal or direct correspondence, not structured findings.
wrong.1: Speeches are written to be spoken, focusing more on flow and impact than rigid sections.
wrong.2: While essays can be factual, reports demand a specific structure involving formal sections like an executive summary.

quiz.say: When writing a speech for your classmates, what should your tone generally be?

options.show: Engaging and appropriate for the group
options.say: Engaging and appropriate for the group

quiz.why: The tone must match the audience; speaking to classmates allows for a more relatable and engaging style.

wrong.0: Overusing slang can make the speech seem unprofessional, even if the audience is informal.
wrong.2: This tone might sound unnatural or overly distant when speaking to peers.
wrong.3: Reading stiffly prevents you from connecting with the audience through natural speaking patterns.

quiz.say: If you write a letter to a company manager, which element is most important for the format?
quiz.why: The address block establishes the professional context and shows you followed standard formal letter conventions.

wrong.0: The conclusion should summarise, not expand upon, the main points already made.
wrong.2: While good, a catchy line does not replace the necessary structural elements of the address.
wrong.3: Exclamation marks are too informal for a professional communication like this.
